Hello everyone, and welcome to another installment of Hullo Talk. We're talking to Ken Dunkley, who is in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Ken, how are you? Oh, great. Great, Frank. It's good to finally have you on the show. Yes, same, actually. I know we did a trip together over the summer, and many of the things that we'll talk about we probably discussed already on the trip. So, it'll probably be review for you, but there's a lot of listeners out there that will be listening to this, and it'll be new to them. Okay, all right. Why don't we start off with having you tell the listeners about how you got involved with Hullography. I know one of your most famous holograms, and I know it's not your only hologram, but certainly the hologram that you will always have. The Hullography Hullography, which will always be remembered for Thoughts, was made while I was still in high school. But how did you get involved with Hullography leading up to making Thoughts? Let's see. Leading up to Thoughts, I was, you know, I saw myself as a photographer. I always carried a camera and did quite a bit of shooting, actually. I think I had gotten to the point where I was, you know, considered myself a sub-professional. And I actually knew professionals at that time who were, you know, shooting professionally at studios in Manhattan. And, of course, I was always studying physics at that time. Were you originally from Philadelphia? I'm originally, no, actually I'm originally from Brooklyn, New York. Brooklyn, New York, okay. Went to school, high school in Heron High School in Manhattan. And spent a lot of time in Manhattan as a youngster after school. And, of course, eventually wound up at New York University studying aeronautical engineering. And I was really into aeronautical engineering, mainly because I had worked with model airplanes since I can remember. Probably about seven, eight years old, I started building models. I built model airplanes and just continued to build them, actually, all through, you know, regular school and then high school. I also, you know, built model airplanes. I got into cameras through my brother, who was and started with cameras. I started with my older brother, so I started with cameras behind him. And so that worked out very well for me. It worked out very well. There are a lot of side stories along the way, and I thought I was leaving. I was leaving them out as to why I did photography, because I had a terrible memory. And I always looked at a camera as my external memory. I see. My onboard, you know, my onboard external memory, so to speak. And your background is in physics, is that correct? My background is physics, because I did three years of aeronautical engineering and then got into physics, and the quantum theory really bugged the hell out of me. It really bugged me. I thought that... A so-called particle can go through two averages at the same time, et cetera, et cetera. You know, the quantum hypothesis, so to speak, really threw me. And a friend, Harry Kamada, and myself, we decided, hey, let's get into some real stuff. So we left the aerodepartment and went into the physics department. I see. And never looked back, actually. Where was Thoughts made? Thoughts was made at New York University. 1970, the summer of 73. Was it a holography lab that was being used for research or for art? Henry Stroke was my advisor, Professor Stroke. It was a spectroscopic laboratory. They had a huge spectrometer. You know, typically a spectrometer is a little box, maybe two feet by three feet. Well, this spectrometer was like 25 feet long. It's 15, 20 feet wide. And it sat. It was specially constructed with concrete columns going 30 feet into the ground, supporting granite tables that supported these huge spectroscopic mirrors. Okay. And they bounced the beam. Then they would take a, I forget what source they used. They used various sources. But they used very, over the years, they did very detailed, hyperfine structure. To look at very small energy levels in certain materials. And they brought me in. And they said, Ken, we have this spectrometer.

very small energy levels in certain materials. And they brought me in and they said, Ken, if you go inside the spectroscopic room, inside, so it's like inside a spectrometer, and if you can set up a hologram on the first table, well, actually it said you should be able to set up a hologram on the first table because those tables are perfectly flat and steady. You're right. We found out years later they weren't, but that's still another story. Is that where you did your experiments as far as drift with air currents? My drift experiments came out later, much later, actually, when I was with Princeton Applied Research. Okay. That was with Princeton Applied Research from 1976 to 1986, a 10-year stretch. And during that time I had the opportunity to travel across the Delaware Valley and monitor everybody's laboratory. I got a seismic accelerometer, a seismic detector, and I sampled, literally, I went to, I had customers. I had all these customers, like Bell Laboratories, I had customers. I had customers at Princeton University. I had customers at the Princeton Applied Physics Labs. I had customers all over the place. I had customers in Philadelphia, whatever. So I actually went around sampling the optical tables of numerous customers and got some idea. And all of this came out of the fact that I was able to create thoughts without isolation. Thoughts was created without, with zero isolation. No kidding. Yeah. I did not know that. Okay. Presumably it was because when we did it, when I did it, all of my holograms up at the New York University, we were all under the assumption, that that place was peculiar because, number one, it's the highest point in the Bronx. It's the highest point in New York City. Excuse me. Okay. In fact, there's a statue that says so as much. That says it because somehow the British troops that came down from somewhere actually came through University Heights, where my lab was. So they built this laboratory at the highest point in New York City that we thought was hollowed ground. And it was a very high level of ground in terms of stability. That was bull. We found out in more than one occasion that that place was no more stable than any other place. And the fact that I was able to make that hologram with no isolation worried the hell out of me because I couldn't figure, because I always thought that, well, I assumed that it was because this place was special. But then of course I measured it and it wasn't. Isn't that something? Yeah, it wasn't. Now, let me let people know because I'll have a photo of it on the Holotalk web page. Okay, great. But it's a laser transmission hologram. Now, one of the things that I did not realize about this piece, I saw this piece for the first time, I believe, in 1979. Images in time and space. I didn't see it in Montreal. In other words, most of the places it went, I couldn't follow. Yeah. So it traveled around the world, but I didn't. And that's when it was damaged at some point. Well, the one thing that I didn't realize is that it's actually a hologram that's recorded in that hologram. Right, right. Yes. I thought there were mirrors in the sand. Well, some people thought that at first, but if you look at it carefully, you realize, no, that can't be a mirror because it's a hologram. It's not reflecting what's in the sand. It's not reflecting. It's not reflecting. But if you look closely, you realize that, well, it can't be a mirror. So it gets into... I did share with... I didn't... At first, it was a secret. I didn't tell anyone how I did that. Oh, okay. But then I think it was either Dan Schweitzer or Sam Moray came at me years later and said, Ken, you know, that hologram of a hologram thing is a lot of... There's something... That still doesn't explain how you did that hook piece. Is that a single beam or a split beam? It's not a single beam. No, it's... It's not a single beam. Okay. In other words, I'm... I guess now after 30-something years, I should tell people how I did it. Oh, yeah.

Maybe you shouldn't. Well, go ahead. Tell people how you did it. Well, no, actually, it turns out that, assuming you know about holography, if you look at it, you still really can't figure it out. If you look at it, you know what it's like? It's like, I'll be honest with you, it's like an optical Chinese puzzle. Notice Chinese puzzles that are like a wood, and you have to move one piece, and then the whole thing comes apart? Yes. Okay, well, I use the beam. There's one beam there that's used for two purposes. Both the reference and illuminating the other hologram? It's essentially that. It's used for two purposes. And it's used in such a way, the geometry is peaked in such a way, that it's really, you can't tell. And at some point, if you know about holography, and you figure it's got to be this, it's got to be that, it's got to be, you cannot figure out, because another thing has to do with the movement of time through the piece. If the time is going in one direction, and the plates have to be assembled in the opposite direction, the whole thing is an optical puzzle going either which way. Okay. And a lot of, most people don't even, realize that. And I've never really talked on it. When you, so it's almost like, when you get to the point where you think you understand it, like, I think it was Sam who came at me and said, that hologram of a hologram stuff doesn't fly. There's something else going on in there. And he was the one that sort of, you know, yeah, it's really tricky that, you know, because time is flowing in two different directions in the piece, within the piece. And they're at odds with each other. And how you have to build it, and how the way the motion of the flow of the image, you look at it, wait a minute, so you're really stuck. Yes. It confuses me sometimes. Well. It amazes me, let me put it this way. It actually amazes me. When I got to that point, when I put it down momentarily, because it was never ever finished, people don't realize that the idea wasn't to do, the idea was to have a series of 20 plates. And I was in a spiral. Oh, I see. In a visual spiral. And what happened was, I ran into a bump in the road. I was supposed to knock this thing out, boom, boom, boom, boom, because I had prepared years for this. I had prepared for years, setting up everything that I needed to do a series of pieces. And the first portion of it went so great, so fast. And the holograms were great eggs, super duper. Brilliant quality. But actually, Thoughts itself is not a grade A hologram, it's grade B. Why do you say that? Well, because it is. Because the thing that I was doing all along worked beautiful. And what happened was, all of a sudden, I could not get a steady exposure on what I had been doing right along. Okay? And I actually worked two months on one plate to get the right exposure. It would not. And then my visor. And then I would walk through the door. Henry would walk through the door and would say, what have you done? He would always go to France, actually, on a sabbatical. And he would walk through the door thinking I had finished, I had come close to finishing this thesis, which I had expanded well beyond, you know, beyond the point. I was doing all of this image smoothing. I created this rotating sequential process that presented images, three images to the eye at a very high rate to smooth it. And then I would think, well, I'm going to do this again. And then I would think, well, I'm going to do this again. I had done all these great things and Henry thought I'd put a rap on this thing. And I walked in and I said, Henry, I got good news and bad news. The bad news was I didn't finish it. I didn't even touch it. The good news was I had this piece. Well, Henry looked at this piece for like five seconds and said, Well, what else are you doing here? I mean, it didn't register within his consciousness. And I knew I was in trouble. Not serious trouble, but it was just, it wasn't good because I didn't, you know, I was supposed to knock out that hologram within weeks. I spent the entire summer on it. Two months on the wall.
